subject: math

unit.title: Statistics, shape and symmetry
unit.essentialQuestion: How do we record data, and how do we describe shapes by their parts and their symmetry?

title: Tally charts and pictograms
objectives: By the end, I can make a tally chart and read a pictogram, including one with a key.

vocabulary.definition: quick counting strokes — four straight, then the fifth goes across like a gate
vocabulary.example: 7 votes = one gate of 5 and 2 more

vocabulary.definition: the fifth tally stroke crosses the four, bundling them into a 5
a chart that uses pictures to show amounts
vocabulary.example: a row of ice creams shows the chocolate votes

vocabulary.definition: the little note that says what ONE picture is worth

emphasize: On a pictogram, read the KEY first — one picture can stand for MORE than one thing.
Pre-empt counting each symbol as 1 when the key says 2 or 5.
The fifth tally stroke crosses the four — the gate makes counting in 5s easy.

keyConcepts: a pictogram's key sets each symbol's value
count symbols, then multiply by the key
misconceptions: counting each pictogram symbol as 1 when the key says 🍦 = 2 or 5
drawing five separate tally strokes with no gate, then miscounting
counting the gates as 4 (forgetting the crossing stroke is the fifth)
hooks: Let's settle a big question — what's the family's favourite ice-cream flavour? Collect the votes and PROVE the winner with a chart.

digital: animated tally strokes on the whiteboard block
pictogram rows built from emoji (table blocks with a key)

plan.goal: Set up the ice-cream survey mission; retrieve counting in 5s (it powers both tallies and keys).
plan.note: Take the child's own vote first — their data, their chart. Quick end-of-unit-6 retrieval too if time allows (quarter to).
plan.successCriteria: Child casts a vote and counts 5, 10, 15, 20 without help.

script.say: Today we settle a BIG question: what's your family's favourite ice-cream flavour? We won't guess — we'll collect everyone's vote and PROVE the winner with a chart. You vote first: chocolate, strawberry or vanilla? … Locked in! Now, detectives need quick counting — count in 5s to 20 for me. Go!
script.adaptHints: Swap ice cream for a survey the child would burn to answer (favourite dinosaur, football team, game). Listen for a clean 5, 10, 15, 20.

blocks.caption: The big vote: which flavour wins?

stuckProtocol: If counting in 5s is shaky: count fingers on whole hands together — one hand is 5, two hands 10 — before going on.

plan.goal: Model tallying with the gate of five, and reading a pictogram by checking the key FIRST.
plan.note: Two tools, one habit each: tally → fifth stroke crosses; pictogram → read the key before counting. Draw the gate stroke by stroke.
plan.successCriteria: Child hears the gate rule and sees 3 symbols with key 🍦 = 2 counted as 2, 4, 6 — six, not three.

script.say: Vote counters use a TALLY. Watch: one, two, three, four straight strokes… and the FIFTH goes across like a gate — snap! That bundle is 5, so I can count in 5s. Now the second tool: a PICTOGRAM uses pictures — but here's the trap. See this little note? It's the KEY, and it says one ice cream stands for 2 votes. So three ice creams isn't 3 — count with me: 2, 4, 6. SIX votes! Always read the key first.
script.adaptHints: Draw the strokes slowly and let the child say 'gate!' on the fifth. Stress the key reveal like a plot twist.

plan.goal: Shared go: the child tallies 7 votes (one gate + 2) and reads a pictogram row with key 🍦 = 2.
plan.note: The character scribes; the child decides the strokes. Then a real pictogram of the flavour survey — child counts a 4-symbol row in 2s.
plan.successCriteria: Child says '7 = one gate and 2 more' and reads 4 symbols with key = 2 as 8.

script.say: Chocolate got 7 votes — you're the tally boss. How do I show 7? … Yes: four strokes, gate on the fifth — that's 5 — then two more. Now here's our survey as a pictogram. The key says one ice cream = 2 votes. Strawberry has 4 ice creams — count them in 2s with me… 2, 4, 6, 8. Eight votes!
script.adaptHints: Let the child call each stroke. If they count symbols as 1 each, don't correct — point back at the key and ask 'what's ONE ice cream worth?'

blocks.caption: Our ice-cream survey — read the key first!

blocks.text: 7 votes = one gate of 5 and ___ more strokes.

check.question: Key: 🍦 = 2. Strawberry's row has 4 ice creams — how many votes?

wrongAnswers.why: counted each symbol as 1 — ignored the key
wrongAnswers.remedy: Look at the key first: what is ONE ice cream worth? Now count the row in 2s.

wrongAnswers.why: counted in 2s but missed a symbol
wrongAnswers.remedy: Touch each ice cream as you count: 2, 4, 6… is that all of them?

plan.goal: The big diagnostic: key 🍎 = 5, a row of 4 apples — 20, not 4.
plan.note: This is the lesson's key trap. '4' means the key habit hasn't landed — re-run 'what's ONE symbol worth' before anything else.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 20 and says they looked at the key first.

script.say: Check time — new chart, new key, eyes sharp! This pictogram's key says one apple stands for 5 children. The 'likes red apples' row has 4 apples. How many children is that?
script.adaptHints: After a correct answer, probe: 'Where did you look first?' — celebrate 'the key' as detective thinking.

blocks.caption: Fruit survey at a school — each 🍎 stands for 5 children

blocks.prompt: Key: 🍎 = 5. The row shows 4 apples. How many children?
blocks.explain: Each apple is worth 5 — count in 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20. Twenty children.

check.question: Pictogram key 🍎 = 5; a row has 4 apples — how many children?

wrongAnswers.why: counted each symbol as 1 — the classic pictogram trap
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read the key: each apple is 5 whole children. Count the row in 5s: 5, 10, 15…

wrongAnswers.why: added the symbols (4) and the key (5) instead of multiplying
wrongAnswers.remedy: The key isn't extra apples — it tells you what EACH apple is worth. Four apples, each worth 5: count 5, 10, 15, 20.

plan.goal: Independent tallying and pictogram reading with keys of 2 and 5; once secure, interleave a half-symbol read.
plan.note: Director draws from the practiceBank, start level 2. Watch for the key being ignored and gateless tallies. Half-symbol items are the level-3 stretch.
plan.successCriteria: Child completes 3+ items correctly, including one tally item and one pictogram with a key bigger than 1.

script.say: Practice time, data detective! Tallies to count, pictograms to crack — and every chart has a key waiting to trick anyone who doesn't read it first. Not you, though.
script.adaptHints: Reframe survey topics around the child's interests (dinosaurs, football, minibeasts). Never change the numbers or the keys.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'I think the key got skipped' or 'the strokes lost their gates.'
Point at the key together and count out ONE symbol's worth on fingers.
Re-ask with key = 2 and a short row, then build back to key = 5.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'

plan.goal: Child states the two habits — gate of five, key first — and the survey winner is crowned; end on a win.
plan.note: Child-led recall; announce the ice-cream winner with ceremony.
plan.successCriteria: Child says 'read the key first' unprompted and explains the gate of five.

script.say: Drumroll… the winning flavour is the one with the most votes on OUR chart — you proved it with real data! Now tell me: what's the FIRST thing you do when you read a pictogram? … And what does the fifth tally stroke do? … Exactly. You checked the key before counting every single time — that's what stops the big pictogram trap.
script.adaptHints: Name the actual winning flavour from the child's survey. Praise the observed process: key first, gates counted in 5s.

block.prompt: A tally shows one gate of 5 and 1 more stroke. How many votes?
block.explain: The gate is 5, plus 1 more stroke — 6.

wrongAnswers.why: counted the gate but forgot the extra stroke
wrongAnswers.remedy: The gate is 5 — now keep counting the loose strokes: 5… and one more?

wrongAnswers.why: counted the gate's standing strokes only, missing the crossing fifth
wrongAnswers.remedy: The stroke lying across IS the fifth vote — the gate always holds 5.

hints: A gate is always worth exactly 5.
Say 5 for the gate, then count on: 6…

reteach.say: A gate is a bundle of five friends — four standing and one lying across. Count the gate as one shout of FIVE, then count the loose strokes on top: 5… 6. Six votes.

block.prompt: You get a brand-new pictogram. What do you look at FIRST?
block.explain: The key tells you what one picture is worth — without it every count could be wrong.

wrongAnswers.why: jumped to comparing before knowing what a symbol is worth
wrongAnswers.remedy: The longest row IS interesting — but how much is each picture worth? Only one thing tells you.

wrongAnswers.why: treating the pictogram as decoration, not data
wrongAnswers.remedy: Every picture is secretly a number. Which part of the chart tells you the secret?

hints: One little note unlocks the whole chart.
It tells you what ONE picture is worth.

reteach.say: The key is the decoder ring. If it says one apple = 2, every apple on the whole chart is worth 2. Skip the key and every answer goes wrong — read it first, always.

block.definition: the note that says what ONE symbol is worth

block.text: Two gates of 5 and no loose strokes = ___ votes.

wrongAnswers.why: counted the gates as objects instead of bundles of 5
wrongAnswers.remedy: Each gate holds 5 votes inside. Two gates: count in 5s — 5, 10.

wrongAnswers.why: counted one gate as 5 and the other as its strokes minus the cross
wrongAnswers.remedy: Every gate is worth exactly 5 — no exceptions. 5 for the first, then 5 more.

reteach.say: Gates make counting fast: don't count strokes one by one, count gates in 5s. Two gates — 5, 10. That's the whole point of the gate!

practiceBank.skill: read a pictogram with a key

block.prompt: Key: 🍦 = 2 votes. The chocolate row has 5 ice creams. How many votes?

wrongAnswers.why: counted each symbol as 1 — ignored the key
wrongAnswers.remedy: Key first! One ice cream is worth 2. Count the row in 2s: 2, 4, 6…

wrongAnswers.why: added the key to the symbol count (5 + 2)
wrongAnswers.remedy: The key isn't added on — it's what EACH picture is worth. Five pictures, each worth 2: count 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.

hints: What is ONE ice cream worth? The key knows.

reteach.say: Each ice cream is secretly TWO votes wearing one coat. Five ice creams: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Ten votes. Touch each picture as you count in 2s and it never goes wrong.

practiceBank.skill: read a pictogram with a key

block.prompt: Key: 🍎 = 5 children. A row shows 3 apples. How many children?

wrongAnswers.why: counted symbols as 1 each
wrongAnswers.remedy: The key says each apple is a whole handful — 5. Count the row in 5s.

wrongAnswers.why: added 3 + 5 instead of counting three 5s
wrongAnswers.remedy: Three apples, EACH worth 5 — that's 5 three times: 5, 10, 15.

hints: One apple = one hand of 5 fingers.

reteach.say: Picture each apple as a high-five — five in every one. Three apples: 5, 10, 15. Fifteen children. The key turns pictures into 5s.

block.prompt: You need to tally 12 votes. How many GATES of 5 will you draw (with 2 loose strokes left over)?

wrongAnswers.why: planned a stroke for every vote with no gates at all
wrongAnswers.remedy: Twelve loose strokes are easy to miscount — bundle them! How many full 5s fit inside 12?

wrongAnswers.why: rounded up — tried to force the last 2 into a gate
wrongAnswers.remedy: A gate needs exactly 5. After two gates you've used 10 — do the last 2 fill a gate?

hints: Count in 5s towards 12: 5, 10… can you fit another 5?

reteach.say: Build 12 the tally way: first gate — 5. Second gate — 10. Another gate would need 5 more, but only 2 votes are left, so they stand alone: gate, gate, stroke, stroke. Two gates and 2 loose.

block.prompt: Match each tally to its total.

wrongAnswers.why: counted the gate as 1 and added 3
wrongAnswers.remedy: A gate is never 1 — it's a bundle of 5. Say FIVE for the gate, then count on the strokes.

hints: Gates first, in 5s — then count on the loose strokes.
2 gates = 10 before you touch the strokes.

reteach.say: Tally counting is a two-step dance: step one, count the gates in 5s — 5, 10. Step two, count on the loose strokes — 11, 12, 13, 14. Gates then strokes, every time.

steps: Count on the loose strokes one by one.

block.prompt: Stretch! Key: 🍦 = 2. A row shows 3 whole ice creams and HALF an ice cream. How many votes?
block.explain: Three wholes are 2, 4, 6 — and half a symbol is half of 2, which is 1. Total 7.

wrongAnswers.why: ignored the half symbol
wrongAnswers.remedy: That half ice cream still counts! If a whole one is 2, what's half of one worth?

wrongAnswers.why: counted symbols as 1 each, half included
wrongAnswers.remedy: Key first — each whole is 2. Count the wholes in 2s, then add half of the key.

hints: Half a symbol = half of the key. Half of 2 is…?

reteach.say: A half symbol is half the key's worth. Key says 2, so half a picture is 1. Wholes: 2, 4, 6. Add the half: 7. If the key said 10, that half would be worth 5!

block.statement: In a pictogram, every picture is always worth exactly 1.
block.explain: The key decides! One picture can stand for 2, 5, 10 — whatever the key says.

wrongAnswers.why: the lesson's core misconception — symbols read as 1 each
wrongAnswers.remedy: Think of our apple chart — one apple stood for 5 whole children. What told us that?

hints: Remember the apple chart — was one apple one child?
Which part of the chart decides a picture's worth?

reteach.say: Pictures are shapeshifters — the same apple can mean 1, 2 or 5 depending on the chart. Only the key pins it down. That's why detectives read the key before counting anything.

block.caption: Same row, different keys — the key rules

block.prompt: A friend reads a pictogram with key 🍎 = 2. The row has 4 apples and they say 'four people'. What went wrong, and what's the real answer?
block.sample: They ignored the key — each apple is worth 2, so it's 2, 4, 6, 8. Eight people, not four.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: They skipped the key; each symbol is 2, so 4 apples = 8 people

wrongAnswers.answer: Nothing went wrong — 4 apples means 4 people
wrongAnswers.why: shares the symbols-worth-1 misconception
wrongAnswers.remedy: Check the key together: what does it say ONE apple stands for? Now count the row in 2s.

wrongAnswers.why: understood the key but miscounted the 2s
wrongAnswers.remedy: Touch each apple and count: 2, 4, 6… is there a fourth apple?

hints: What did the friend forget to read first?

reteach.say: The friend fell straight into the pictogram trap: counting pictures instead of what pictures are WORTH. The key says each apple carries 2 people. Four apples: 2, 4, 6, 8. Explaining the trap to a friend means you've truly beaten it!

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave tally items and pictogram items (and mix keys of 2 and 5).
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run that item's reteach, count ONE symbol's worth out on fingers together, then serve a level-1 item of the same skill.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 3+ correct across levels 2–3 including one tally item and one pictogram item with key ≥ 2 → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'tally charts and pictograms'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: key skipped, or tally gates lost.
Point at the key and count one symbol's worth together on fingers.
Re-ask with key = 2 and a short row, then build back to key = 5.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: Rebuild the survey around the learner's world (LearnerModel.interests): favourite dinosaurs, football teams, ice-cream flavours. Keep the keys and counts identical.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a winnable read (key = 2, short row), then specific process praise: 'you read the key before counting, every single time — that's real data-detective work.'

differentiation.support: Key = 2 only; finger on each symbol while counting in 2s; tallies capped at two gates; the key stays highlighted on screen.
differentiation.stretch: Half-symbol reads (half the key's value); design a pictogram from a tally and CHOOSE a sensible key for big numbers.

extension: Chart designer — turn the ice-cream tally into a pictogram with the child's own key (would 🍦 = 2 or 🍦 = 5 make a neater chart? Why?).
assessmentEvidence: Child tallies accurately with gates of five and reads pictograms with keys of 2 and 5 by multiplying, not counting symbols as 1.
revisitLater: Data reading continues immediately in Lesson 22 (block diagrams); bring back one key = 5 pictogram read in the Lesson 25 quiz.
